articles.title: A FastAPI admin panel with Jinja and HTMX, without an admin framework
articles.excerpt: A SaaS admin panel isn't really a database browser. It's a few screens that answer "who is this customer, what are they paying for, and can I help them?". That's small enough to build with ordinary Fa…
articles.body: A SaaS admin panel isn't really a database browser. It's a few screens that answer "who is this customer, what are they paying for, and can I help them?". That's small enough to build with ordinary FastAPI routes, Jinja templates and a few HTMX attributes, and it gets the same CSRF protection, sessions and tests as the rest of your app. Why not an admin framework? Libraries like SQLAdmin generate list and edit screens for your models, and for internal CRUD over many tables they're a good fit. A SaaS panel has different needs. The useful operations aren't "edit this row" but "deactivate this account and sign it out everywhere" or "give this partner the Pro plan until March".

articles.title: I built PROOF: a tool to verify AI-generated apps with real browser tests
articles.excerpt: Building software with AI coding agents is incredibly fast. But I kept running into a frustrating problem: The AI says the task is complete. The code compiles. The tests pass. But does the application…
articles.body: Building software with AI coding agents is incredibly fast. But I kept running into a frustrating problem: The AI says the task is complete. The code compiles. The tests pass. But does the application actually work? That question inspired me to start building PROOF , a tool that turns real browser tests into visual evidence. 🔍 What is PROOF? PROOF is a local web application that uses Playwright to verify user interactions and generate reports showing exactly what was tested. Instead of relying only on statements like "all tests passed," I wanted a way to see the actual results. The current prototype can: Execute configurable browser tests. Interact with real web applications. Verify specific success conditions. Capture screenshots during execution. Identify failed verification steps.

articles.body: Kubernetes AI conformance gives an operator a listing, not an acceptance record. A listing says a vendor filed a statement against a versioned checklist and that the statement sits in the program's repository. An acceptance record says the evidence behind that statement is sufficient for a named workload, on a named platform, at a named Kubernetes version. This post reads the 24 submissions filed against Kubernetes v1.35, states what the program establishes about them and what it leaves open, and sets out where the operator's own test begins. Everything below is bound to one repository state and one version.

articles.title: My memory guard watched one process grow to 268 GB and did nothing, because it trusted the agent
articles.excerpt: Yesterday at 2:37 PM, macOS showed "Your system has run out of application memory" on my Mac. I run Claude Code all day, and I also run a guard that watches for runaway processes. The guard checked ev…
articles.body: Yesterday at 2:37 PM, macOS showed "Your system has run out of application memory" on my Mac. I run Claude Code all day, and I also run a guard that watches for runaway processes. The guard checked every minute during the whole incident. It stopped nine small leftover processes. It never touched the one that caused the problem. Between 2:25 and 2:36 PM, a single node helper running under Claude grew from about 10 GB to 268 GB of memory footprint. Swap reached 76 GB. Why the guard missed it The guard's rules were written around a real fear: killing an agent while you are using it. So the rule was simple. If a process belongs to a live agent session, leave it alone. That protects a Claude or Codex session that is working hard on a big build.

articles.title: 'It looked like every star in the sky was falling': Eyewitnesses remember the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966
articles.excerpt: It was a spectacle many regard as the greatest meteor display on record.
articles.body: Overnight Nov. 17-18, 1966, the Leonid meteor storm thrilled stargazers during one extraordinary night when the stars themselves looked as though they were falling from the sky. At the peak of the shower, observers at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona estimated an astonishing 40 meteors per second streaking across the sky. That's 2,400 shooting stars per minute, or a staggering 144,000 per hour. It was a spectacle that many regard as the greatest meteor display in recorded history. It's hard to imagine what it was like to experience such a spectacle. But who better to tell us than those who saw it with their own eyes? To mark the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, we asked those who saw it to share their memories.
articles.author: Daisy Dobrijevic

articles.body: More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye. That's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that currently circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). Analyzing data from Oct. 12 and 18 this year, researchers found that with a completely unobstructed horizon, 710 satellites were crossing the sky in every single moment of the night above an average U.K. town. The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S. Space Force available through the public website CelesTrak.
